**The Twice-Daily Country**

There is a strip of the world that belongs to nobody in particular, because it cannot decide what it is. For six hours or so it is land: rock, sand, weed drying to a crust, small crabs picking their way between puddles. Then, for six hours or so, it is sea. Then land again. It goes on doing this without pause and without an audience, and has done so for something like four billion years, which is longer than anything has been alive to notice.

I want to write about the intertidal zone, and about tides generally, partly because I find them beautiful and partly because they are one of the few enormous facts about the planet that a person can stand and watch happen. Continental drift is real but you will never see it. The precession of the equinoxes is real but you would need twenty-six thousand years and a very good chair. The tide, though, will come in while you eat a sandwich. You can put a stick at the water's edge and go for a walk and come back and the stick will be gone, or newly exposed, and in either case the planet has moved a vast mass of water past you while you were thinking about something else.

---

The mechanism is not quite the one most people carry around. The common picture is that the moon pulls the ocean toward itself, and so there's a bulge of water on the moon-facing side of the earth. That's half right. There is a bulge there. But there is also a bulge on the far side, the side facing away from the moon, and this is the part that trips people up, because it looks as if the moon must somehow be pushing the water away.

It isn't. The moon pulls on everything—on the near ocean, on the solid earth beneath it, on the far ocean—but it pulls hardest on what's closest. So the near water is tugged toward the moon a little more than the earth is, and the earth is tugged toward the moon a little more than the far water is. Relative to the planet, the near ocean leans in and the far ocean is left behind. Two bulges. The earth rotates underneath them once a day, so most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides in roughly twenty-four hours and fifty minutes—the extra fifty minutes being the moon's own progress along its orbit, which means the earth has to turn a little further each day to catch up.

The sun does the same thing at a little under half the strength. When sun and moon line up—new moon and full moon—their bulges stack and you get spring tides, the highest highs and lowest lows. When they're at right angles, at the quarter moons, they partly cancel, and you get neap tides, which are timid and don't go far in either direction. The word *spring* here has nothing to do with the season; it's the old sense of springing up, welling. Sailors and fishermen have known this alignment for as long as there have been sailors and fishermen, long before anyone could explain it.

---

Explaining it took an astonishingly long time. The Mediterranean, where a good deal of Western thinking got done, has almost no tides worth mentioning—a few centimeters here and there, easily mistaken for wind. So Greek philosophers grew up with a sea that simply sat in its basin, and when their travelers came back from the Atlantic with stories of the ocean rising and falling by the height of a house, twice a day, the stories were filed with the other things travelers said.

Pytheas of Massalia sailed north to Britain around 325 BC and came back reporting enormous tides and, remarkably, connecting them to the moon. He was widely disbelieved. Around the same time, Alexander's fleet under Nearchus, resting at the mouth of the Indus, was caught by a tidal surge that lifted and stranded the ships and terrified soldiers who had crossed half the known world without encountering anything like it. Aristotle, characteristically, wanted a cause and reached for winds and the earth's breathing. Various later writers proposed that the ocean was a living thing inhaling and exhaling, or that the moon heated the water and made it swell.

The first person in the English-speaking world to write carefully about tides was, of all people, a monk. Bede, at Jarrow on the Tyne in the early eighth century, lived beside a river that filled and emptied with the sea, and he paid attention. In *The Reckoning of Time* he not only ties the tides firmly to the moon but notices something subtler: that high tide comes at different hours at different places along the coast, and that each port has, in effect, its own fixed delay relative to the moon's passage. This idea—later called the establishment of the port—is the basis of every tide table since. Bede was working out how to compute the date of Easter, which requires knowing where the moon is; he seems to have simply looked up from his calculations and out the window.

It would be nearly a thousand years before Newton supplied the gravitational account, and longer still before anyone could predict tides at a given harbor with real precision. The problem is that the simple two-bulge picture is a fiction for a water-covered sphere. Real oceans have basins, shelves, straits, and coastlines, and the tidal bulge slops around inside them like water in a carried bathtub. The Bay of Fundy, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, happens to have a natural sloshing period close to the tidal period, so the tide there resonates and can rise and fall by sixteen meters, the height of a four-story building. Some places, where two tidal waves arrive out of phase, have almost no tide at all. The actual water at any real harbor is the sum of dozens of overlapping rhythms—the moon's daily pull, the sun's, the moon's changing distance, the tilt of its orbit, a fortnightly cycle, a monthly one, an 18.6-year wobble—each with its own amplitude for that specific bit of coast.

In the 1870s William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, built a brass machine to add these rhythms up. It was essentially a row of pulleys, each driven by a gear turning at the period of one tidal component, with a single wire threaded over all of them; the wire's total displacement was the sum of the parts, and a pen at the end drew the predicted tide curve on a roll of paper. You turned a handle and a year's worth of tides came out. Refined versions of these machines were still in use in the twentieth century. The tide predictions for the Normandy landings in June 1944 were computed on one at the Liverpool Tidal Institute, because the planners needed to land at a low-enough tide to expose the German beach obstacles but a high-enough one that the men wouldn't have to cross too much open sand. The moon, in other words, was consulted, via a brass analog computer, on the timing of the largest amphibious invasion in history.

---

There is a rule of thumb that anyone who spends time near the sea eventually learns, called the rule of twelfths. Take the total range between low and high water and divide it into twelve parts. In the first hour after low tide the water rises one twelfth. In the second hour, two twelfths. In the third and fourth, three twelfths each. Then two, then one. The tide, in other words, comes in slowly, then fast, then slowly, in the shape of a sine wave sliced into hours.

What this means in practice is that the middle two hours are dangerous. If you're walking on a broad flat beach at the beginning of the rise, the water seems to be creeping. Around hour three it is not creeping. On a very flat shore, where a vertical rise of a few centimeters translates into a horizontal advance of many meters, the sea can move in faster than a person walks, and it does not come in as a neat line but fills the low channels first, so that what looked like beach becomes a set of islands and then no islands at all.

Morecambe Bay, on the northwest coast of England, is the textbook case. It is a vast shallow expanse of sand and mud, some 120 square miles at low water, threaded with river channels that shift from one week to the next. There has been an official guide to walking across it since the sixteenth century—the post is called the Queen's Guide to the Sands, or King's now, and is paid a nominal sum by the Duchy of Lancaster. The most famous holder, Cedric Robinson, led groups across for fifty-six years, probing the sand ahead with a stick to find the quicksand, and marking the safe route with laurel branches. In 2004, twenty-three Chinese migrant workers gathering cockles in the bay at night, without a guide and without knowing the sands, were cut off by the incoming tide and drowned. The tide is not malevolent. It is exactly as predictable as the machine at Liverpool said it was. It is only indifferent, and indifference on that scale is its own kind of terrible.

---

But I want to come back to the strip itself, the twice-daily country, because it is where the strangeness gets concentrated.

Consider what it is to live there. Twice a day you are underwater and twice a day you are in the air. If you're in the air at low tide on a summer afternoon, you are baked, and the small pool you're sitting in is turning to brine as it evaporates. If low tide falls in the rain, that same pool is diluted toward fresh water. In winter you may be frozen. Then the sea comes back and everything is reset to cold, salty, and moving, with waves that can hit rock with the force of a truck. Most habitats specialize in one hostile condition. The intertidal alternates between several, on a schedule.

Almost everything that lives there has solved this with some combination of clinging on and closing up. Barnacles are the extreme case. They look like tiny volcanoes of limestone but they are crustaceans, relatives of crabs and shrimp; as larvae they swim free, then choose a spot, glue their heads to it with one of the strongest natural adhesives known, and build a shell around themselves. For the rest of their lives they stand on their heads and kick food into their mouths with their legs when the water is in, and close their little hatches and wait when it's out. Limpets, the conical snails you find fastened to rock, wander a short way to graze on algae when the tide covers them, and then return—to the exact same spot, a "home scar" their shell has worn to fit—before the water drops. Nobody is entirely certain how they navigate back. Mussels tie themselves down with threads. Periwinkles seal their doors with mucus and go dormant. Seaweeds simply go limp and lie there, slick and rubbery, and let the drying happen to their outer layers while the inner ones wait.

And then there are the pools, which are the intertidal's showpieces. A tide pool is a hostage situation: everything in it was going about its business in a continuous ocean and is now confined to a basin the size of a sink until the sea returns. Anemones pull in their tentacles and become dull blobs, or don't, and sit open in the still water like flowers that have wandered into the wrong kingdom. Small fish that would be unremarkable in open water become, in a pool, individuals; you can watch one for twenty minutes. Hermit crabs conduct their real-estate disputes. A shore crab retreats under a ledge and regards you. The whole scene has the clarity of an aquarium but none of the artifice, and it will be dismantled in a few hours and reassembled somewhere slightly different tomorrow.

The zones stack up the shore in bands, because different creatures can tolerate different amounts of time out of water. At the top, where only the highest spring tides reach, lichens and a few tough periwinkles. Below that, barnacles. Below that, the limpets and mussels and the brown wracks. Lower still, the red algae and the anemones and the things that can only stand a couple of hours of air. Walking down a rocky shore at low water is walking through these horizons one at a time, like descending through strata in a cliff, except the strata are alive and the elevation difference between them might be a meter.

---

There is one more thing about tides that I find hard to stop thinking about, and it's this: they are slowing the earth down.

The tidal bulges don't sit exactly under the moon. Friction with the ocean floor and the rotation of the planet drag them slightly ahead. The moon pulls back on that displaced bulge, and the effect is a tiny braking of the earth's spin, and a corresponding shove that lifts the moon into a slightly higher orbit. The numbers are small. The day lengthens by about two milliseconds per century. The moon recedes by about three point eight centimeters a year, roughly the rate your fingernails grow. But the earth has had a lot of centuries.

We know this not only from theory but from rock. In certain places, tidal sediments were laid down in layers that record the daily and fortnightly rhythms, and by counting them the way one counts tree rings, geologists can read off how many days there were in a month, and a year, hundreds of millions of years ago. Coral growth bands tell a similar story. Four hundred million years ago, in the Devonian, the day was around twenty-two hours long and there were about four hundred of them in a year. Go back far enough and the moon hangs much closer and larger in the sky, the tides are far more violent, and the day is a handful of hours. Every low tide you have ever seen was, in a sense, slightly later and slightly gentler than the ones before it, on a timescale no one can feel.

Some biologists have wondered whether the intertidal—that strip that is alternately drowned and dried—was the training ground for the move onto land. It's hard to prove. But it is at least a pleasing thought that the first creatures to spend a few hours a day out of the water might have been doing so not by choice but because the ocean kept leaving them behind, twice a day, until they got used to it.

---

I said the intertidal belongs to nobody because it can't decide what it is. I've been turning that around, and I think it is closer to say that it is the one place that is honest about being two things. Most of the world is also in flux; it just hides it better. The shoreline puts the cycle on display at a human scale, with a schedule printed in the newspaper.

There are causeway islands—Lindisfarne, off Northumberland, is one; Mont-Saint-Michel in Normandy is the grand version—where a road across the sands is dry for a few hours and then simply gone. Lindisfarne keeps a small hut on stilts halfway across for drivers who misjudge it. People misjudge it every year, standing in the box with their shoes wet, watching their car fill up, waiting for the sea to go away so they can walk home. The tables were right. They were published. The moon was exactly where it was supposed to be. And there is something in me that finds that not depressing but consoling: that a thing so large should be so regular, and that its regularity should be so completely uninterested in whether I've noticed. It will be low water again in about six hours. The stick will reappear. The limpets will be home.
